title: Act II, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: From the orchard Romeo sees Juliet at her window and calls her the sun. Unaware of him, she wishes he were not a Montague. He speaks; she fears for his life, worries he will think her too forward, and asks him not to swear by the inconstant moon. They exchange vows; Juliet proposes he send word tomorrow of when and where they will marry.

Next, craft. I notice the metaphor, light in darkness, which recurs through the play. The strongest word is “sun”: it makes her the center of his world, giving life and light. Then, effect. What does Romeo's comparison of Juliet to the sun show? My answer: Romeo's love makes Juliet radiant and essential to him; the light imagery prepares the play's pattern of lovers who meet in darkness.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for imagery, characterization (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the balcony scene? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act II, Scene II develops the idea of the balcony scene. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Juliet is the more clear-sighted lover in the balcony scene. When the text says “What’s in a name? that which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet” (Act II, Scene II, Juliet), it shows this directly. She sees that their vow "is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden; / Too like the lightning," and she reasons that "that which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet," while Romeo speaks in raptures.
